title: What will you worship after me
hookLine: the dying Ya'qub asks his sons, and they answer, your God and the God of your fathers (2:133)
carry: what will you keep after me
last: PRAY FOR THE ONES NOT BORN.

lines: AN OLD MAN, HIS SONS AROUND THE BED.
cards: At a bedside near the end, the last conversations tend to be short, and about what matters. The mortgage doesn't come up. They ask: are you going to be all right?
Will you look after your sister? Do you remember what I taught you? Al-Baqarah takes us into a room like that: an old man, his sons gathered around the bed, and one question.
Today: what will you worship after me.

teach.h: WERE YOU THERE WHEN DEATH CAME?
teach.b: The old man is Ya'qub, Ibrahim's grandson, also called Israel.
The verse before says Ibrahim had given his sons a charge, and Ya'qub did the same: God has chosen the religion for you, so don't die except in submission to Him.
Then verse one hundred thirty-three asks the listener directly: were you there when death came to Ya'qub? And it lets us in.

teach.h: WHAT WILL YE WORSHIP AFTER ME?
teach.b: He says to his sons, in Pickthall's words: “What will ye worship after me?” Not what will you do with the flocks, not who gets what. The one thing he wants to know before he goes.

teach.h: A CHAIN OF NAMES, BOTH BRANCHES
teach.b: They answer with a chain of names: we will worship your God, the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq, one God, and to Him we submit. Notice one name.
Isma'il isn't Ya'qub's father; he's his uncle, the brother of his father Ishaq. The commentators point out that Arabic can count an uncle among the fathers.
The sons name both branches of the family in one breath, as one line of faith.
In Islamic tradition, a deathbed charge like this has a name: wasiyyah, a counsel, a will.

Muslims are encouraged to write a will for their property, and some also leave words for their families about prayer, kindness and keeping ties. Ya'qub's charge was already given. At the very end, he doesn't repeat it.
He asks, and lets his sons say it in their own voices.

how: Muslims are encouraged to prepare a wasiyyah, a will, and some add words of counsel for their families about faith and conduct, following the example of Ibrahim and Ya'qub in al-Baqarah.

a last counsel, a will left for those after you

games.why: what will you worship after me? he has already given them his charge; at the end he asks, and they answer in their own voices.

practice: Think of someone who will carry something of you after you, a child, a niece, a student, a younger friend, and ask what one thing you hope they keep: not a possession, but a habit, a way of treating people, a word, a faith.
Put it into one plain sentence and hold it quietly.

wordCard.voice: Wasiyyah. A last counsel, a will — Ya'qub's deathbed charge to his sons, asking what they would worship after him. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a last counsel, a will; 2:132 uses the same root for the charge Ibrahim and Ya'qub gave their sons.
